You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# ARC object-relation audit

Use this class-level checklist when a grid contains distinct objects in multiple colors, sparse singleton cells, or examples whose changed object is not obvious.

## Workflow
1. Segment non-background cells into objects/components; record each object's color, bounding box, shape, and singleton/line status.
2. Compare every demo input and output cellwise. Record changed cells and which object(s) changed; explicitly record conspicuously unchanged objects as negative evidence.
3. Test relational hypotheses before local shape-copy hypotheses: a marker may encode a target color or select an object by color, shape, adjacency, or position. Check whether the same relation predicts the changed object across demos with different palettes and layouts.
4. State competing hypotheses and the test prediction each implies. Request another demo only if a specific outcome discriminates them and could change the prediction.
5. Verify the complete predicted output, preserving all untouched cells and objects, before submission.

## Recurrence: task-561fb912 (mixed demos; previous solves unresolved)

### Confirmed rule from an additional solved instance
In one instance, a partially occluded/irregular `6` motif occurred twice: a 3-cell horizontal bar at the upper-left and a 3-cell horizontal bar at the lower-right, with corresponding second-row shape pieces. Both were changed to the same color as the separate horizontal 5-cell line (color 3); other objects remained unchanged. Input details: rows 0–1 near cols 6–8 had 6s (`row0 c6-8`, `row1 c7-8`); rows 14–15 near cols 17–19 had 6s (`r14 c17-19`, `r15 c18-19`). Output changed these 6s to 3, retaining all else. The first submitted identity-like grid was rejected because it kept the target shapes as 6. The corrected output recolored those motif cells to 3 and was accepted.

This supports a relation in that instance: recolor the repeated motif matching the color-3 line object's pattern/role to color 3, while preserving unrelated shapes. It is not a general task-wide rule; earlier examples had assorted sparse recolorings. For future recurrences, carefully compare repeated/related objects with line or shape cues; do not blindly map every component or assume color mapping without demo support.

## Recurrence: task-561fb912 (mixed demos; previous solves unresolved)
This task family is sparse selective recoloring amidst noisy multicolor shapes and line/corner markers. The selection criterion may depend on larger structures; do not guess by source color or component size. Historical examples were inconsistent and insufficient to establish one general rule. One prior instance was accepted after recoloring selected broad bar-shaped objects based on a 1D geometric relationship; another remained unsolved. Treat demonstrations as evidence to build a task-specific predicate, not a fixed mapping.

### Confirmed current instance: task-561fb912
Test grid 13x24; output kept dimensions and all original cells except two contiguous color-6 structures changed to color 5:
- horizontal 4-cell segment at row 5, columns 7-10 (0-based indexing);
- two vertical 2-cell segments: rows 6-7, col 9-10 (these form a 2x2 component at rows 6-7, cols 9-10), plus? Exact changed cells are row 5 cols 7-10 and rows 6-8? Verify source/output from accepted submission: row6 cols7,9,10 changed to 5; row7 cols9,10 changed to 5. Other 6s unchanged.
The accepted output recolored the color-6 horizontal bar immediately adjacent/parallel to the long color-5 horizontal bar (the demo context suggests selecting an object aligned with / matching long-bar shape cues), while leaving other 6 components untouched. It also changed nearby color-6 shapes to 5 as explicitly encoded in accepted grid. Exact accepted cells: row5 c7-10; row6 c7,c9,c10; row7 c9,c10. Do not overgeneralize this without validating demos; prior recurrence confirms uncertainty.

Current session demos (8) and outputs: demo1 changed only a vertical 4-cell component of color 8 at rows 11-14? to 3; demo2 changed a 2x2-ish color-7 component at top-left to 5; demo3 changed a two-cell color-2 vertical component to 5; demo4 changed a 2x2 color-3 object to 7; demo5 changed a bottom-center color-3 component to 9; demo6 changed a lower-left color-3 component to 8; demo7 changed the lower color-5 silhouette to 0; demo8 changed two color-9 cells to 3. These only establish sparse recolorings, not a reliable universal selection rule.

Operational rule: preserve all else; replay full demos and detect any common geometric relation before reusing. Avoid serial demo requests without synthesis.

## Pitfalls
- Do not infer a stamping operation just because a large shape and isolated markers coexist.
- Avoid serial demo requests without analyzing exact changes and updating hypotheses after each pair.
- A rule is not validated until it explains both changed and unchanged objects across every demo.
- In protocol-constrained ARC, send exactly one action JSON object per turn.
